WordPress vs Webflow for Contractors: Which Wins?

Unbiased comparison of WordPress vs Webflow for contractors. Includes real cost data, speed benchmarks, SEO capabilities, migration guidance, and lead...

OnwardCraft Team Growth Strategists

Most platform comparisons are written by people selling one of the platforms. This one is not.

We are a marketing agency that builds contractor websites on both WordPress and Webflow. We have no incentive to push you toward either platform. Our only goal is to help you choose the one that generates more leads for your specific contracting business.

Here is what you will learn in this guide:

  • The real total cost of ownership for each platform (including the costs nobody talks about)
  • Actual Core Web Vitals speed data from 2025 benchmarks
  • Which platform converts more website visitors into leads
  • How each platform handles local SEO for contractors
  • Exactly how to migrate from one platform to the other without losing rankings
  • When Wix or Squarespace might actually be the better choice
  • A decision framework that tells you which platform to choose in under 5 minutes

Let us start with how we evaluated both platforms.

Chapter 1: How We Evaluated Both Platforms

We scored WordPress and Webflow across seven criteria that directly impact a contractor's ability to generate leads online. These are not abstract technical metrics. They are the factors that determine whether a homeowner who finds your website actually fills out a quote form or calls your number.

Our Seven Evaluation Criteria

Criterion Why It Matters for Contractors
Lead Generation Capability Can the platform support fast quote forms, click-to-call, CRM integration, and conversion tracking?
Mobile Performance 60-70% of contractor website traffic comes from mobile devices. Slow mobile sites kill leads.
SEO Flexibility Can you optimize for "near me" searches, service area pages, and local schema markup?
Ease of Updates Can you add a new service page or change your phone number without calling a developer?
Total Cost of Ownership What do you actually pay over 3 years, including hosting, plugins, maintenance, and developer time?
Support & Ecosystem When something breaks on a Sunday, can you find someone to fix it?
Scalability Will the platform handle 50 location pages, 200 project photos, and a growing blog?

The Data Sources Behind This Comparison

Every claim in this guide is backed by one or more of the following:

  • HTTP Archive Chrome UX Report (through November 2025) — real user performance data from millions of websites
  • Hostingstep Core Web Vitals Study 2025 — CMS-specific benchmark analysis
  • Codeable WordPress Maintenance Pricing Report 2026 — real market pricing data
  • W3Techs market share data (March 2026) — platform usage statistics
  • Our own agency data from building contractor websites on both platforms since 2019

We do not use manufacturer-provided speed scores or marketing claims. We use real-world data from actual websites running on these platforms.

Chapter 2: WordPress for Contractors — The Full Picture

WordPress powers approximately 43% of all websites on the internet and holds 62-65% of the CMS market share, according to W3Techs data from early 2026. For contractors, it represents the most flexible and widely supported option — but flexibility comes with responsibility.

What WordPress Actually Is

WordPress is open-source software. You download it for free, install it on a web host, and build your site using themes and plugins. There is no single company controlling it. The WordPress Foundation, a non-profit, oversees the core software. Thousands of developers contribute code. This decentralization is both WordPress's greatest strength and its biggest weakness.

For contractors, the critical distinction is between WordPress.org (self-hosted, which we discuss here) and WordPress.com (a hosted service run by Automattic). Most contractor websites run on WordPress.org because it offers full control.

The Pros of WordPress for Contractors

1. Unmatched Plugin Ecosystem

WordPress has over 60,000 plugins in its official repository, plus thousands more from third-party developers. For contractors, this means you can add almost any functionality without custom coding:

  • Lead capture: WPForms, Gravity Forms, and Fluent Forms support multi-step quote forms, conditional logic, and file uploads for project photos.
  • Local SEO: Rank Math SEO and Yoast SEO offer granular control over local business schema, service area pages, and Google Business Profile integration.
  • Reviews: Plugins like WP Business Reviews and TrustIndex pull reviews from Google, Yelp, and Facebook directly onto your site.
  • Booking: Amelia and Simply Schedule Appointments let homeowners book consultations online.
  • CRM integration: WP Fusion connects WordPress to HubSpot, Salesforce, Zoho, and dozens of other CRMs.

No other platform comes close to this level of extensibility.

2. Complete Ownership and Portability

With WordPress, you own your files and database. If you are unhappy with your host, you can move to another one in a few hours. If your developer disappears, you can hire another one — there are thousands of WordPress developers in every major city.

This matters for contractors because your website is a business asset. You do not want it trapped on a platform you cannot leave.

3. Superior Content Marketing Scalability

Contractors who invest in content marketing — blog posts about "how to prepare your roof for winter" or "signs your HVAC system needs replacement" — need a platform that makes publishing easy. WordPress was built for blogging. Its editorial workflow, media library, and content organization tools are still the best in the industry.

A roofing contractor publishing 2-3 blog posts per month, 50+ service area pages, and 100+ project case studies will find WordPress far more efficient than Webflow's CMS.

4. Lower Long-Term Costs (If Managed Well)

WordPress core software is free. Basic shared hosting starts at $5-10 per month. With careful plugin selection and a lightweight theme, a contractor can run a fast, effective website for under $300 per year.

The key phrase is "if managed well." We will cover what happens when it is not managed well in the cons section.

5. Better Local SEO Tooling

Rank Math SEO Pro and Yoast SEO Premium offer features specifically designed for local businesses:

  • Multiple location schema markup
  • Service area page optimization
  • Local business structured data
  • Integration with Google Business Profile
  • Internal linking suggestions

Webflow has built-in SEO tools, but they lack the depth and specialization that contractors need for local search dominance.

The Cons of WordPress for Contractors

1. Maintenance Is Not Optional

WordPress requires ongoing maintenance. Core updates, theme updates, and plugin updates happen constantly. In the first half of 2025 alone, Patchstack identified over 6,700 new vulnerabilities in WordPress plugins and themes. Forty-one percent of those were exploitable in real-world attacks.

A 2025 survey by Melapress found that 96% of WordPress professionals have encountered security incidents, and 64% have dealt with full website breaches. Only 27% had a recovery plan in place.

For a contractor who would rather be on a job site than managing a website, this is a serious liability.

2. Performance Varies Wildly

According to HTTP Archive data analyzed by Hostingstep in 2025, only 43% of WordPress.org websites pass Core Web Vitals on desktop, and just 35% pass on mobile. That is significantly below the global average of 53%.

The reason is not WordPress itself. It is how most people set it up: cheap shared hosting, bloated page builder themes (Elementor and Divi add 200-600KB of render-blocking JavaScript), and 20-30 active plugins fighting with each other.

A well-optimized WordPress site on quality hosting can achieve sub-1.8-second Largest Contentful Paint and 85-95 PageSpeed scores. But that requires technical knowledge or a managed hosting budget of $200+ per month.

3. The Hidden Cost of Plugins

Premium plugin subscriptions add up quickly:

Plugin Category Typical Annual Cost
SEO (Rank Math Pro or Yoast Premium) $99-$199
Page builder (Elementor Pro) $59-$399
Security (Wordfence Pro) $99
Backup (UpdraftPlus Premium) $70-$145
Forms (Gravity Forms) $59-$259
Image optimization (Smush Pro) $60-$120
Total (mid-range stack) $446-$1,221/year

These are recurring annual costs. Miss a renewal, and your site loses functionality.

4. The Plugin Conflict Problem

Every plugin you add increases the risk of conflicts. Two plugins that work fine independently can break each other after an update. Debugging these conflicts requires technical expertise. A contractor without a developer on call can find their contact form broken for days before noticing.

5. Steeper Learning Curve for Non-Technical Users

The WordPress block editor (Gutenberg) has improved significantly, but it is still less intuitive than Webflow's visual editor. Customizing layouts, adjusting responsive breakpoints, and styling elements without breaking the theme requires either a page builder plugin (which hurts performance) or CSS knowledge.

Real Contractor WordPress Examples

Northface Construction (Minnesota) — Built on WordPress with a custom theme. Features emotional headline copy, GAF Master Elite certification badges, and strong local SEO. The site ranks #1 for "roofing contractor Minnesota" and generates an estimated 80-120 leads per month.

Thelen Mechanical (Michigan) — WordPress site with clear benefit messaging, seasonal promotions, and integrated booking. The $89 HVAC check-up offer is prominently displayed above the fold.

Chapter 3: Webflow for Contractors — The Full Picture

Webflow is a visual website builder and CMS that generates clean HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Unlike WordPress, it is a closed, all-in-one platform. You design visually, and Webflow handles hosting, security, updates, and CDN delivery automatically.

Founded in 2013, Webflow has grown to power approximately 4 million websites with a 0.9% share of all websites (W3Techs, March 2026). While smaller than WordPress, it is the fastest-growing developer-focused website builder, with 12.5% year-over-year growth.

What Webflow Actually Is

Webflow combines a visual design tool (similar to Adobe Photoshop or Figma) with a content management system and hosting infrastructure. You design by dragging elements onto a canvas, adjusting properties in panels, and setting responsive breakpoints visually. Webflow then generates production-ready code and hosts it on AWS with Fastly CDN.

For contractors, the appeal is simple: you get a fast, secure, visually impressive website without managing servers, updates, or plugins.

The Pros of Webflow for Contractors

1. Superior Out-of-the-Box Performance

Webflow websites consistently outperform WordPress sites on Core Web Vitals without any optimization work:

Metric Webflow (Median) WordPress (Standard) Winner
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) 2.1-2.4s desktop 3.2-3.8s Webflow
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) 0.04-0.06 0.12 Webflow
Time to First Byte (TTFB) 72% pass rate 32% pass rate Webflow
Desktop CWV Pass Rate 79% 43% Webflow
Mobile CWV Pass Rate 67% 35% Webflow

Source: HTTP Archive Chrome UX Report, Hostingstep 2025 analysis

This performance gap directly impacts lead generation. Google research shows that a 1-second delay in mobile load time reduces conversion rates by 7%. For a contractor generating 50 leads per month at $500 average value, a 1-second improvement could mean an additional $1,750 in monthly revenue.

2. Zero Maintenance Burden

Webflow handles everything: server management, security patches, SSL certificates, DDoS protection, CDN configuration, and backups. You never log in to find 17 plugin updates pending. You never wake up to a hacked website. You never troubleshoot why your contact form stopped working after a theme update.

For contractors who want a "set it and forget it" website, this is Webflow's killer feature.

3. Visual Design Control Without Code

Webflow's designer lets you create custom layouts, animations, and responsive behaviors visually. You are not limited to pre-built templates or theme options. A contractor who wants a unique portfolio showcase with hover effects, scroll-triggered animations, and custom grid layouts can build it without writing code.

Real Webflow contractor sites like DHE Contractors and Revolution Contractors demonstrate this design flexibility with bold hero images, custom service navigation, and professional photography integration.

4. Clean, Semantic HTML Output

Webflow generates clean HTML that search engines easily understand. There is no bloated page builder markup, no jQuery dependencies, and no plugin-injected scripts cluttering the page. This clean code foundation gives Webflow a structural SEO advantage.

5. Built-In Hosting, CDN, and Security

Every Webflow site includes:
- AWS hosting with automatic scaling
- Fastly CDN for global content delivery
- Free SSL certificates
- DDoS protection
- Automatic daily backups
- Two-factor authentication

These features would cost $50-200 per month as add-ons for a WordPress site.

6. Predictable Pricing

Webflow's pricing is straightforward:

Plan Monthly Cost (Annual) Best For
Basic $14 Simple static sites
CMS $23 Blogs, content sites (2,000 CMS items)
Business $39 High-traffic sites (10,000 CMS items)
E-commerce Standard $29 Up to 500 products
E-commerce Plus $74 Up to 5,000 products

No surprise plugin renewal bills. No hosting upgrade fees when traffic spikes. No security plugin subscriptions.

The Cons of Webflow for Contractors

1. The CMS Item Limit

Webflow's CMS plan allows 2,000 total content items across all collections. This includes blog posts, portfolio projects, testimonials, team members, and service pages. For a growing contractor adding 50 projects per year, 30 blog posts per year, and 100 testimonials, the 2,000-item limit becomes a real constraint within 3-5 years.

The Business plan increases this to 10,000 items at $39 per month. Enterprise plans offer up to 1 million items but require custom pricing.

For comparison, WordPress has no content limits. A contractor can publish 100,000 pages without platform restrictions.

2. Limited Plugin and Integration Ecosystem

Webflow has approximately 300 integrations, compared to WordPress's 60,000+ plugins. For contractors who need specialized functionality — advanced quoting calculators, project management integrations, or custom CRM workflows — Webflow often falls short.

Webflow does support custom code embeds and third-party tools via Zapier, but these workarounds are less elegant than native WordPress plugins.

3. Vendor Lock-In

You cannot export a Webflow site and host it elsewhere while preserving functionality. While Webflow allows HTML/CSS export, the CMS, forms, and dynamic content do not export. If Webflow raises prices, changes terms, or goes offline, migrating away requires rebuilding the site.

With WordPress, you own everything. Your database, your files, your content. You can move hosts, switch developers, or modify the code however you want.

4. Thinner Local Developer Pool

Need a quick fix on a Sunday? WordPress developers are everywhere. Webflow experts are harder to find and often charge premium rates. According to agency data from Blott.com, custom WordPress theme development takes 200+ hours, while Webflow reduces development time by 50% — but only if you have someone who knows Webflow.

5. E-Commerce Transaction Fees

Webflow's Standard e-commerce plan charges a 2% transaction fee on top of payment processor fees (2.9% + $0.30). For a contractor selling products or large-ticket services online, this adds up. WooCommerce on WordPress charges zero platform transaction fees.

Scenario Webflow Standard (2% fee) WooCommerce (0% fee) Difference
$100,000 annual sales $2,000 platform fee $0 Webflow costs $2,000 more
$250,000 annual sales $5,000 platform fee $0 Webflow costs $5,000 more

Webflow's Plus and Advanced e-commerce plans eliminate the transaction fee but cost $74 and $212 per month respectively.

6. Steeper Initial Learning Curve

Webflow's visual designer is powerful but complex. Non-designers often find the interface overwhelming. G2's comparison data estimates Webflow's learning curve at approximately 4 hours for a simple site, while WordPress takes 10-12 hours for basic proficiency but offers a shallower long-term learning curve for content updates.

Speed Comparison: The Real Data

Let us be specific about what "fast" means in 2025.

Google's Core Web Vitals are the standard. Here is how each platform performs based on real user data from the Chrome UX Report:

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — How fast the main content loads:
- Webflow median: 2.1-2.4 seconds (desktop), 2.5-3.5 seconds (mobile)
- WordPress median (standard): 3.2-3.8 seconds (desktop), 3.5-5.0 seconds (mobile)
- WordPress median (optimized on Kinsta/WP Engine): 1.6-1.8 seconds

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — Visual stability:
- Webflow: 0.04-0.06 (excellent)
- WordPress: 0.12 (needs improvement)

Webflow wins on CLS because layouts are pre-computed at publish time. WordPress themes often load fonts, images, and ads dynamically, causing layout shifts.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — Responsiveness to user input:
- Webflow: 190-210ms
- WordPress: 280ms+ (standard), lower with optimization

The Verdict on Speed:

Webflow delivers consistent, good performance without effort. WordPress can be faster than Webflow but only with premium hosting, lightweight themes, and ongoing optimization. For a contractor without a technical team, Webflow's "good enough by default" speed is the safer choice.

SEO Comparison: Which Platform Ranks Better?

This is the question every contractor asks, and the answer is nuanced.

Technical SEO Foundation:

Webflow has the better technical foundation out of the box. Clean HTML, automatic sitemaps, built-in SSL, fast CDN, and minimal render-blocking resources. A Webflow site with default settings has better technical SEO than a default WordPress install.

On-Page and Local SEO Depth:

WordPress wins for advanced SEO work. Rank Math SEO Pro offers:
- Local business schema with multiple locations
- Service area page optimization templates
- Automated internal linking suggestions
- Advanced breadcrumb control
- 404 monitor and redirect manager
- SEO analysis for every page

Webflow has basic meta title/description editing, automatic sitemaps, and canonical tags. Advanced schema markup requires custom code injection. Creating 50 location pages for a multi-city contractor requires duplicating pages manually or using CMS collections with workarounds.

Content SEO Scale:

A contractor publishing 3 blog posts per week, 10 service pages, and 50 city pages will find WordPress far more efficient. The block editor, media library, category system, and editorial workflow are built for content production at scale.

Webflow's CMS is elegant for smaller sites but becomes cumbersome with high content volume. The 2,000-item limit on the CMS plan is a hard ceiling.

The Verdict on SEO:

For a single-location contractor with a simple site, Webflow's technical foundation may provide a slight ranking advantage. For a multi-location contractor investing in content marketing and local SEO, WordPress's tooling and scalability are superior.

Mobile Comparison: Where Most Contractor Leads Originate

Sixty to seventy percent of contractor website traffic comes from mobile devices. Emergency services like plumbing and HVAC see even higher mobile percentages — homeowners with a burst pipe search on their phones.

Webflow Mobile Strengths:
- Responsive breakpoints are set visually and precisely
- Touch-friendly interactions by default
- Fast mobile loading with automatic image optimization
- No plugin-generated mobile bloat

WordPress Mobile Challenges:
- Page builders (Elementor, Divi) often generate heavy mobile markup
- Plugin scripts load on mobile even when not needed
- Responsive behavior depends on theme quality
- Mobile optimization requires additional plugins (AMP, mobile-specific caching)

The Verdict on Mobile:

Webflow delivers better mobile performance with less effort. WordPress can match it, but only with a lightweight theme, minimal plugins, and mobile-specific optimization.

Ease of Use Comparison

Making Content Updates:

WordPress's block editor is functional but can be frustrating. Formatting inconsistencies, theme conflicts, and plugin shortcodes create a learning curve. A contractor who wants to change a phone number or add a new service page can usually do so after 2-3 hours of training.

Webflow's editor mode is more visual and consistent. What you see is what you get. However, the full designer interface is complex, and making structural changes requires understanding CSS concepts like flexbox and grid.

The Verdict on Ease of Use:

For simple content updates (text changes, photo swaps, blog posts), Webflow is more intuitive. For structural changes and advanced customization, WordPress offers more paths to success — but with more ways to break things.

Chapter 5: Other Platforms Worth Considering

WordPress and Webflow are not the only options. Depending on your situation, Wix, Squarespace, or custom development might be the better choice.

Wix for Contractors

Best for: Solo contractors who need a website live by tomorrow and have zero technical skills.

Pros:
- Fastest setup of any platform (AI can build a site in minutes)
- 900+ templates, many for home services
- App marketplace with contractor-specific tools
- 24/7 support
- Improved Core Web Vitals (71% pass rate on desktop, up from 57% in 2024)

Cons:
- Template-locked once published (cannot switch templates without rebuilding)
- Bloated code that hurts advanced SEO
- Limited design flexibility
- Cannot export your site

Cost: $16-27/month for business plans. No transaction fees.

Verdict: Wix is fine for contractors who just need a digital business card. It is not suitable for contractors serious about organic lead generation or content marketing.

Squarespace for Contractors

Best for: Design-focused trades like interior remodeling, landscaping, or custom carpentry where visual impression drives leads.

Pros:
- Stunning templates with cohesive design systems
- Built-in scheduling (Acuity integration)
- Strong mobile responsiveness
- Good for portfolio showcase

Cons:
- Rigid grid layouts limit customization
- Limited third-party integrations
- Mediocre SEO tools compared to WordPress
- 70% desktop CWV pass rate, 53% mobile

Cost: $16-49/month. No transaction fees on standard plans.

Verdict: Squarespace works for contractors where aesthetics are the primary differentiator. For lead generation and local SEO, WordPress or Webflow are stronger.

Custom Development

Best for: Large contracting firms with unique workflow needs, complex quoting systems, or integration requirements that no platform handles natively.

Pros:
- Complete control over every aspect
- No platform limitations
- Can integrate with any system

Cons:
- $10,000-$50,000+ initial investment
- Requires ongoing developer relationship
- Longest time to launch

Verdict: Custom development is overkill for 95% of contractors. Choose it only when you have validated that no platform can meet your specific requirements.

Chapter 6: Migration Guide — Switching Platforms Without Losing Rankings

If you are already on one platform and considering a switch, this chapter is critical. A poorly executed migration can destroy years of SEO progress. A well-executed migration can improve performance while preserving rankings.

WordPress to Webflow Migration

Step 1: Pre-Migration Audit (1-2 weeks before)

Export a complete inventory of your URLs using Screaming Frog or Sitebulb. Document:
- Every page URL
- Meta titles and descriptions
- Heading structures (H1-H6)
- Image alt text
- Internal link map
- Top-performing pages (from Google Search Console)
- Baseline traffic and ranking data

Step 2: Plan Your URL Structure

Keep identical URL slugs whenever possible. If /services/roofing-repair/ works on WordPress, use the same slug on Webflow. Consistent URLs eliminate the need for redirects and preserve link equity.

If URLs must change, create a complete 301 redirect map:

Old URL (WordPress) New URL (Webflow)
/services/plumbing/ /services/plumbing/
/blog/winter-prep/ /blog/winter-prep/
/about-us/ /about/

Step 3: Migrate Content

Webflow does not have a direct WordPress import tool. You will need to:
- Export WordPress content to XML
- Use a tool like PowerImporter or manually copy content
- Re-upload images to Webflow's asset manager
- Rebuild page structures in Webflow's designer

For CMS content (blog posts, projects, testimonials), use Webflow's CSV import feature or a third-party migration service.

Step 4: Rebuild Technical SEO Elements

Element How to Handle in Webflow
Meta titles/descriptions Enter manually per page; use CMS fields for dynamic content
Heading structure Rebuild semantically; style visually after structure is correct
Image alt text Re-upload images; add alt text in asset manager
Schema markup Add custom JSON-LD in page <head> settings
Open Graph tags Set in page settings
Canonical tags Add global canonical URL
Internal links Update all links to point to new Webflow URLs

Step 5: Implement 301 Redirects

In Webflow: Site Settings → Hosting → 301 Redirects

Bulk import is available via the Finsweet Extension for Chrome. Test every redirect before going live.

Step 6: Launch and Monitor

  1. Submit the new sitemap to Google Search Console
  2. Request indexing for priority pages
  3. Monitor daily for 2 weeks, then weekly for 90 days:
  4. Crawl errors (404s)
  5. Indexing issues
  6. Impression and click fluctuations
  7. Test page speed via Google PageSpeed Insights
  8. Reinstall tracking (Google Analytics, Tag Manager, conversion pixels)
  9. Keep WordPress running for 90 days as a fallback

Expected Timeline:
- Initial traffic fluctuation: 2-4 weeks
- Full reindexing: ~30 days
- Rankings stabilization: 60-90 days
- Performance improvements: Visible by month 2-3

Normal traffic fluctuation is 10-20%. A drop exceeding 30% requires immediate investigation.

Webflow to WordPress Migration

Step 1: Export Content

Webflow allows CMS content export to CSV. Export all collections (blog posts, projects, testimonials, team members).

Static page content must be copied manually or via web scraping tools.

Step 2: Choose WordPress Hosting and Theme

For contractors migrating from Webflow, we recommend:
- Hosting: Kinsta, WP Engine, or Flywheel ($30-100/month)
- Theme: GeneratePress, Kadence, or Astra Pro (lightweight, fast)
- Page builder: Bricks or Breakdance (cleaner code than Elementor)

Step 3: Import Content

Use WordPress's built-in importer or plugins like WP All Import to bring in CSV data. Map Webflow fields to WordPress custom fields or post types.

Step 4: Rebuild Design

This is the most labor-intensive step. Webflow's visual design does not translate directly to WordPress. You have three options:

  1. Match the design closely using a page builder (time-intensive but preserves brand consistency)
  2. Use a pre-built contractor theme and adapt your content (faster, some design compromise)
  3. Hire a developer to build a custom theme matching your Webflow design ($2,000-5,000)

Step 5: SEO Preservation

  • Maintain URL structure where possible
  • Implement 301 redirects via .htaccess or a redirect plugin (Redirection, Rank Math)
  • Transfer all meta titles, descriptions, and schema markup
  • Rebuild internal links
  • Submit new sitemap to Google Search Console

Step 6: Post-Launch Monitoring

Follow the same monitoring protocol as WordPress to Webflow migrations. Expect 60-90 days for full stabilization.

Migration Cost Estimates

Migration Direction DIY Cost Professional Agency Cost Timeline
WordPress → Webflow $0-200 (tools) $2,500-5,000 2-4 weeks
Webflow → WordPress $100-500 (hosting + tools) $3,000-7,000 3-6 weeks
Either → Wix/Squarespace Not recommended N/A N/A

Important: Do not attempt a migration during your busy season. If you are a roofing contractor, migrate in December or January, not after a hail storm.

Chapter 7: Decision Framework — Which Platform Should You Choose?

By this point, you understand the trade-offs. This chapter gives you a clear decision framework.

Choose WordPress If...

  • You plan to publish regular blog content (2+ posts per month)
  • You need 50+ pages or location-specific landing pages
  • You want advanced local SEO control (schema, service areas, multiple locations)
  • You need specialized contractor plugins (quoting tools, CRM integration, booking systems)
  • You have access to technical support (in-house or agency)
  • You want full ownership and portability of your website
  • You are comfortable with ongoing maintenance or can afford a maintenance plan ($100-300/month)
  • Your budget is tight upfront, and you are willing to invest time in learning

Choose Webflow If...

  • You want a visually impressive portfolio site that loads fast
  • You have no technical staff and want minimal maintenance
  • Your site is primarily informational (services, gallery, contact, about)
  • Speed-to-launch matters more than custom functionality
  • You value enterprise security without effort (SSL, DDoS, 2FA included)
  • You want predictable monthly costs without surprise plugin bills
  • Design quality and visual differentiation are priorities
  • You publish content infrequently (less than 2 posts per month)
  • Your total content needs will stay under 2,000-10,000 items

Choose Wix If...

  • You need a website live this week
  • You have zero technical skills and no budget for a developer
  • Your site is a simple digital business card (5-10 pages)
  • You do not rely on organic search for leads

Choose Squarespace If...

  • Visual impression is your primary differentiator
  • You need built-in appointment scheduling
  • You want a cohesive design without customization

Choose Custom Development If...

  • You have unique workflow requirements no platform handles
  • Your budget exceeds $10,000 for initial development
  • You have an in-house development team

The Contractor-Specific Recommendation

After building contractor websites on both platforms for six years, here is our honest assessment:

For most single-location contractors (plumbers, electricians, HVAC, roofing, remodeling):

Start with Webflow if you have the budget for professional setup ($2,000-4,000). The performance advantage, zero maintenance, and visual quality will generate more leads than a poorly maintained WordPress site. The 2,000-item CMS limit will not be a constraint for years.

For multi-location contractors and franchises:

WordPress is the better long-term choice. The ability to create unlimited location pages, integrate with multi-location SEO tools, and scale content production outweighs the maintenance burden. Budget $200-400 per month for managed hosting and maintenance.

For contractors investing heavily in content marketing:

WordPress wins. The editorial workflow, plugin ecosystem, and content organization tools are purpose-built for publishing at scale. A contractor publishing 3-5 blog posts per week will be far more productive in WordPress.

For contractors with no technical resources:

Webflow is the safer choice. The all-in-one nature eliminates the risk of a broken plugin taking your site down on a Saturday. The predictable costs make budgeting easier.

Chapter 8: Getting Started — Your Next Steps

Regardless of which platform you choose, here is how to move forward.

If You Choose WordPress

Week 1:
- Select managed hosting (Kinsta, WP Engine, or Flywheel)
- Choose a lightweight theme (GeneratePress, Kadence, or Astra)
- Install essential plugins: Rank Math SEO, WPForms, Wordfence, UpdraftPlus
- Set up Google Search Console and Google Analytics 4

Week 2-3:
- Build core pages: Home, Services, About, Contact, Service Areas
- Configure local business schema markup
- Set up click-to-call phone numbers and quote forms
- Optimize for Core Web Vitals (image compression, caching, script deferral)

Month 2-3:
- Launch with 5-10 service pages
- Begin publishing blog content (1-2 posts per week)
- Build citations on contractor directories
- Set up review generation system

Ongoing:
- Weekly plugin and core updates
- Monthly performance audit
- Quarterly content and SEO review

If You Choose Webflow

Week 1:
- Sign up for a CMS or Business plan
- Select a contractor template or begin custom design
- Plan your CMS collections (services, projects, testimonials, team)
- Set up Google Search Console and Google Analytics 4

Week 2-3:
- Build core pages in the designer
- Configure CMS collections and populate initial content
- Add custom schema markup via code injection
- Set up forms and connect to your email/CRM

Month 2-3:
- Launch with optimized core pages
- Add 5-10 project portfolio items
- Configure 301 redirects if migrating from another platform
- Submit sitemap to Google Search Console

Ongoing:
- Monthly content updates via the editor
- Quarterly design and performance review
- Annual plan evaluation (upgrade if approaching CMS limits)

When to Hire Help

Hire a developer or agency if:
- Your time is worth more than $100 per hour
- You need custom functionality (quoting tools, CRM integration)
- You are migrating from another platform
- You want advanced SEO implementation
- You need the site live within 2 weeks

DIY if:
- You have technical aptitude and time
- Your site needs are simple (5-10 pages)
- You are comfortable learning the platform
- Your budget is under $1,000

FAQ Section

Is WordPress or Webflow better for SEO?

WordPress offers more advanced SEO tools through plugins like Rank Math and Yoast, including granular local SEO control, schema markup templates, and internal linking suggestions. Webflow has a stronger technical SEO foundation out of the box with clean code and fast performance. For contractors doing basic local SEO, Webflow's built-in tools are sufficient. For contractors investing in content marketing and multi-location SEO, WordPress provides more depth.

How much does it cost to build a contractor website on WordPress vs Webflow?

A professional contractor website costs $2,000-5,000 on either platform for custom design. Ongoing costs differ: WordPress typically runs $100-300 per month including hosting, plugins, and maintenance. Webflow runs $23-39 per month with minimal additional costs. Over three years, WordPress is cheaper for simple sites ($1,500-2,500 total), while Webflow is often cheaper for complex sites ($3,500-6,000 total) because maintenance is included.

Can I migrate my WordPress site to Webflow without losing rankings?

Yes, if you follow SEO best practices. Maintain identical URL structures where possible, implement 301 redirects for any changed URLs, transfer all meta titles and descriptions, rebuild schema markup, and submit the new sitemap to Google Search Console. Expect 10-20% traffic fluctuation for 2-4 weeks, with full stabilization in 60-90 days. Keep your WordPress site running for 90 days as a fallback.

Which platform loads faster for mobile users?

Webflow loads faster out of the box. According to 2025 HTTP Archive data, 67% of Webflow sites pass mobile Core Web Vitals compared to 35% of WordPress sites. However, a well-optimized WordPress site on premium hosting can match or exceed Webflow's speed. The difference is that Webflow achieves good mobile speed automatically, while WordPress requires deliberate optimization.

Do I need a developer to maintain a WordPress website?

Not necessarily, but it helps. Basic WordPress maintenance — updating plugins, backing up, and monitoring security — can be learned by a non-technical person in a few hours. However, when plugin conflicts occur, security incidents happen, or performance issues arise, having a developer available saves significant time and stress. Professional WordPress maintenance services cost $100-300 per month.

Is Webflow too limited for a growing contractor business?

It depends on your growth trajectory. Webflow's CMS plan allows 2,000 content items, which is sufficient for most contractors for 3-5 years. The Business plan increases this to 10,000 items at $39 per month. If you anticipate needing more than 10,000 pages, posts, or portfolio items, WordPress's unlimited scalability is the better choice. For most single-location contractors, Webflow's limits will not be a constraint.

Can I accept online payments on both platforms?

Yes. WordPress uses WooCommerce (free plugin) with payment gateways like Stripe and PayPal. There are no platform transaction fees — you pay only the payment processor's fee (typically 2.9% + $0.30). Webflow has built-in e-commerce with Stripe integration. The Standard plan charges an additional 2% platform fee on top of processor fees. The Plus and Advanced plans eliminate the platform fee but cost $74 and $212 per month respectively.

Which platform is easier for non-technical contractors to update?

Webflow's editor mode is more intuitive for simple content updates like text changes, photo swaps, and blog posts. The visual interface shows exactly how changes will look. WordPress's block editor has improved but can be inconsistent depending on the theme and plugins installed. For structural changes and design customization, both platforms require learning, but Webflow's visual designer is more powerful once mastered.

What happens if Webflow goes out of business?

This is a valid concern given Webflow's closed platform model. While Webflow is well-funded and growing (12.5% YoY), you do not own the underlying infrastructure. Webflow allows HTML/CSS export of static pages, but CMS content, forms, and dynamic features do not export. With WordPress, you own all files and the database and can move to any host. For risk-averse contractors, WordPress's open-source model provides more long-term security.

Should I use Wix or Squarespace instead?

Wix and Squarespace are viable for contractors with simple needs. Wix is best for fast setup and beginners. Squarespace is best for visually focused trades. However, both platforms have significant limitations for serious lead generation: Wix has bloated code and template lock-in; Squarespace has rigid layouts and limited SEO tools. For contractors who rely on organic search for leads, WordPress or Webflow are stronger choices.

How long does it take to build a contractor website on each platform?

A basic 5-10 page contractor website takes 1-2 weeks on Webflow (using a template) or 2-4 weeks on WordPress (depending on theme customization). A custom-designed site takes 4-8 weeks on either platform. Webflow's visual designer can accelerate the design phase, while WordPress's theme ecosystem can accelerate setup for simpler sites.

Can I integrate my CRM with WordPress and Webflow?

WordPress offers superior CRM integration through plugins. WP Fusion connects to HubSpot, Salesforce, Zoho, Pipedrive, and 50+ other CRMs. Gravity Forms and WPForms also have native CRM integrations. Webflow supports CRM integration through Zapier, Make (formerly Integromat), and native forms webhooks. For complex CRM workflows, WordPress provides more direct and robust options.

Which platform do you recommend for a brand-new contracting business?

For a new contractor with a limited budget and no technical support, Webflow on a CMS plan ($23/month) with a quality template ($79) is the safer starting point. The low maintenance burden and fast performance let you focus on running your business, not managing a website. As you grow and your needs become more complex, you can migrate to WordPress or upgrade within Webflow.

How do I track which platform generates more leads?

Set up identical conversion tracking on both platforms before and after migration. Use Google Analytics 4 with conversion events for form submissions and phone clicks. Add call tracking through CallRail or WhatConverts. Measure lead volume, cost per lead, and lead quality for 90 days after any platform change. The platform that delivers lower cost per lead at equal or better quality is the winner for your business.

Is it worth switching from WordPress to Webflow?

Switch from WordPress to Webflow if: your WordPress site is slow despite optimization efforts, maintenance is consuming too much time, you want better design control without a developer, or your site is relatively simple (under 50 pages). Do not switch if: you rely heavily on plugins for business operations, you publish content frequently, you have complex local SEO needs, or you value platform independence.
